title: Lesson 19: Building a Personal Prompt Library
description: How to capture the prompts that already worked, give them enough metadata to find again in seconds, and stop rewriting the same working instructions every time a recurring task rolls around.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Building a Personal Prompt Library", what separates a pile of saved prompts from an actual library?
options: The metadata: a name, a phrase that says when to use it, and a note about what to check in the output
The software or app you store the prompts in
The total number of prompts in the collection
questions.explanation: The lesson says without the metadata you have a pile of prompts, and with it you have a library, because the metadata is what lets you find and use the right prompt.

questions.question: The lesson defines a "working prompt." What makes a prompt a working prompt?
options: It is long and highly detailed
It already produced an output you used and were happy with, so it has been tested in your actual job
It follows a formal template with placeholders
It was written by a colleague rather than by you
questions.explanation: The lesson says the word worked is doing the real work in that phrase: a working prompt has been tested in your job, not just imagined, which is what makes the library trustworthy.

questions.question: How does the lesson frame the payoff of building the library?
options: It removes the need to check outputs before you use them
It replaces your judgment with a saved template
Writing a good prompt from scratch costs thirty to sixty seconds every time plus the risk of forgetting a hard-won detail, and the library changes that math through compounding
It only pays off for tasks you perform twice a year
questions.explanation: The lesson works through the cost of rewriting a good prompt from memory for every recurring task and concludes the payoff shows up later, in the compounding.
